content: The process of measuring wheelchair provision involves systematically collecting data on service users, personnel, service delivery, and the products provided. Evaluation entails analyzing this data and using other methods to assess whether wheelchair provision meets, exceeds, or falls short of established targets. Strengthening the system involves making necessary adjustments when evaluations reveal weaknesses. The primary audience for these guidelines includes stakeholders involved in planning, delivering, monitoring, and evaluating wheelchair provision. This group encompasses policymakers, wheelchair service personnel, and organizations representing wheelchair users. The guidelines are built on four key principles. First, access to an appropriate wheelchair is a fundamental human right, as recognized by the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and other rights-based frameworks like the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. Second, wheelchair provision services should be people-centered, emphasizing user engagement and choice rather than treating individuals as passive recipients. Third, wheelchair provision should be integrated into universal health coverage (UHC), ensuring that all individuals who need wheelchairs can access them without financial hardship. This aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those focused on health, education, and reducing inequalities. Fourth, access to appropriate wheelchairs must be equitable, ensuring fair and just systems that provide support to all individuals in need, regardless of factors like gender, age, socioeconomic status, or geographic location. The development of these guidelines followed the World Health Organization (WHO) methodology, led by a 16-member Guidelines Development Group (GDG) and supported by a WHO Steering Group and an External Review Group. Recommendations were based on a systematic review of evidence, combined with practice-based and lived experiences. Each recommendation was evaluated for its benefits, harms, human rights implications, sociocultural acceptability, health equity, feasibility, and economic considerations. The guidelines aim to support equitable access to appropriate wheelchairs by providing clear recommendations for member states to develop or enhance wheelchair provision systems. Implementation of these guidelines will help governments fulfill their obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and achieve the SDGs, particularly those related to health, education, and reducing inequalities. The scope of the guidelines focuses on the provision element of the WHO-GATE 5P framework, which emphasizes people-centered strategies for increasing access to assistive technology. The recommendations address optimizing service delivery models, delivering core wheelchair services, training personnel, gathering and evaluating data, and creating supportive policy environments. The guidelines are relevant to all countries, wheelchair users, and types of wheelchairs, including manual, powered, and power-assisted devices, as well as essential components like cushions and postural supports. They are not intended to provide detailed clinical or technical guidance on wheelchair selection, fitting, or use but emphasize the need for access to a range of quality wheelchairs and related products. The development process included input from diverse stakeholders, systematic reviews, and evidence evaluation using the GRADE framework. The guidelines were finalized through multiple review rounds and approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee in May 2023. They are expected to remain valid until 2028, with a review planned by the WHO Department of Health Products, Policy, and Standards. The rationale for these guidelines stems from the global disparity in wheelchair provision practices and policies. While some countries have advanced frameworks, global benchmarks for service quality are lacking, and equitable access remains a significant challenge. The guidelines build on previous efforts, such as the 2008 WHO guidelines on manual wheelchairs in less-resourced settings, and aim to address the broader needs of all wheelchair users across various contexts. The guidelines align with other WHO documents and initiatives, including the Global Report on Assistive Technology and the World Report on Disability. They complement the 2008 guidelines while expanding their scope to include all types of wheelchairs and user populations.
